summary: Psalm 124 is a communal thanksgiving that looks back on a danger that could have destroyed Israel. The poem repeats that Yahweh was “on our side,” imagines the threat as attackers, floodwaters, teeth, and a trap, then ends by naming Yahweh, maker of heaven and earth, as Israel’s help.
whyItMatters: This short psalm shows how Book V teaches rescued people to turn survival into shared speech. As a Song of Ascents, it belongs among pilgrimage songs that give a worshiping community words for memory, danger, and help.

context.author: The heading says, “By David,” but Psalms headings can indicate authorship, association, dedication, or belonging; readers differ on how much historical detail this heading establishes.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping community, and later Jewish and Christian communities that adopted the Psalms for public prayer and private life.
context.date: The Psalms were composed and collected over time; the exact date of Psalm 124 is uncertain.
context.setting: Book V of Psalms, within the Songs of Ascents collection. The poem speaks as Israel looking back on a severe but unspecified threat.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and communal thanksgiving, using repetition and vivid images of attack, flood, prey, and escape.

outline.heading: The community is invited to remember
outline.note: The psalm twice says that Yahweh was on Israel’s side when people rose against them.

outline.heading: What might have happened
outline.note: The danger is pictured first as being swallowed alive and then as overwhelming waters going over the soul.

outline.heading: Blessing for rescue
outline.note: Yahweh is blessed because Israel was not handed over as prey, and the escape is pictured as a bird freed from a broken snare.

outline.heading: The final confession of help
outline.note: The psalm ends by locating Israel’s help in Yahweh’s name, identifying Yahweh as maker of heaven and earth.

keyVerses.text: A Song of Ascents. By David. If it had not been Yahweh who was on our side, let Israel now say,
keyVerses.why: This opening gives the heading and sets the poem’s communal voice: Israel is asked to say aloud what would have happened without Yahweh’s help.

keyVerses.text: Blessed be Yahweh, who has not given us as a prey to their teeth.
keyVerses.why: The psalm turns from imagining destruction to blessing Yahweh for rescue.

keyVerses.text: Our soul has escaped like a bird out of the fowler’s snare. The snare is broken, and we have escaped.
keyVerses.why: This verse gives the chapter’s most concrete rescue image: a trapped life set free because the trap itself is broken.

keyVerses.text: Our help is in Yahweh’s name, who made heaven and earth.
keyVerses.why: The closing line gathers the psalm’s confidence into a compact confession of help from the creator.

themes: Help from the maker of heaven and earth

questions.question: Who is speaking in this psalm?
questions.answer: The poem speaks in the first-person plural: “our side,” “against us,” and “we have escaped.” Verse 1 also says, “let Israel now say,” so the voice is communal rather than only private.

questions.question: What does “A Song of Ascents” mean here?
questions.answer: The heading places this psalm within the Songs of Ascents, Psalms 120–134. These songs belong to Book V, where pilgrimage, thanksgiving, Torah, and praise are prominent. The heading helps locate the poem, but it does not by itself tell us the exact first occasion when it was sung.

questions.question: Does “By David” prove David wrote it?
questions.answer: The heading associates the psalm with David, and many readers understand that as authorship. The Hebrew heading construction can also mark association, dedication, or belonging, so readers differ. A careful reading treats the heading as real evidence while acknowledging that it does not settle every question about authorship.

questions.question: What danger is the psalm remembering?
questions.answer: The chapter does not name a specific battle, enemy, date, or event. It says that “men rose up against us,” that their wrath burned, and that Israel would have been swallowed or overwhelmed without Yahweh’s help. The images are vivid, but the historical occasion remains unnamed in the poem.

questions.question: Are the waters literal floodwaters or a poetic image?
questions.answer: The chapter compares the threat to waters that would have overwhelmed the people and gone over their soul. The psalm does not pause to identify an actual flood, so the safest reading is that flood imagery expresses danger that felt overpowering. Readers may compare other biblical water images, but this chapter itself keeps the event unnamed.

questions.question: What does “soul” mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: In the World English Bible text, “soul” appears in the danger image and in the escape image. The poem uses it for the life or self of the community under threat: the waters would have gone over “our soul,” but “Our soul has escaped.” It is not explaining a theory of the soul; it is describing threatened life rescued from danger.

questions.question: Why does the psalm use images of teeth, a bird, and a snare?
questions.answer: The images make the rescue concrete. Verse 6 imagines Israel as prey not given to teeth, and verse 7 imagines a bird escaping a fowler’s snare. Together they show danger as both violent attack and entrapment, while emphasizing that escape has already happened.

questions.question: What does the final line add after the rescue images?
questions.answer: Verse 8 moves from the memory of escape to a general confession: “Our help is in Yahweh’s name.” It also names Yahweh as the one “who made heaven and earth,” so the rescuer of this community is identified as creator, not merely a local helper for one crisis.

questions.question: Does this psalm say faithful people are never threatened?
questions.answer: No. The whole poem assumes a real danger: people rose against Israel, wrath was kindled, and the threat is pictured as waters, teeth, and a snare. The psalm’s claim is not that danger never comes, but that this community survived and blesses Yahweh for not giving them over.

glossary.def: The divine name used throughout this psalm for Israel’s God.
The named community invited in verse 1 to speak the psalm’s memory of rescue.
The anger of the attackers in verse 3, pictured as kindled against the community.
A bird-trap image in verse 7 used to describe danger and escape.
